title: Node.js: JavaScript outside the browser
goal: Understand what Node is, run scripts with arguments, and build your first command-line tool.

concepts: Node = V8 engine + system APIs (files, network, processes); no DOM
The global process: argv, env, exit codes, cwd()
ES modules in Node ("type": "module") and built-in modules with the node: prefix
Reading user input with readline/promises
stdout, stderr and exit codes (0 = success)
Node's event loop is the same idea as the browser's

resources.title: Node.js: How to read environment variables

build.task: Create a NEW repo node-playground with "type": "module" in package.json. Build tip.js, a CLI tip calculator: node tip.js 1250 --tip 15 --split 3 prints the tip, total and per-person amount in ₹. Validate arguments (print usage to stderr and exit with code 1 on bad input). If no arguments are given, ask interactively with readline/promises. Then write sysinfo.js that prints Node version, OS platform, CPU count, free memory in MB and the current folder, using node:os and process.
acceptance: tip.js works with arguments and interactively
Bad input prints a usage message to stderr and exits with code 1 (check with echo $? or $LASTEXITCODE)
Money formatted with Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN')
sysinfo.js prints all 5 facts using node:os and process
README explains how to run both

hints: process.argv is ['path/to/node', 'path/to/tip.js', ...yourArgs], so use process.argv.slice(2). Node's built-in util.parseArgs can parse --tip and --split for you.
Exit with an error: console.error('Usage: node tip.js <amount> [--tip 10] [--split 1]'); process.exit(1);

Interactive: import * as readline from 'node:readline/promises'; const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout }); const a = await rl.question('Bill amount: '); rl.close();

explainBack.q: What's the difference between JavaScript in the browser and in Node?
lookFor: Node has file system, process, network servers

explainBack.q: Why print errors to stderr and exit with code 1?
lookFor: scripts and CI check exit codes
stderr separates errors from normal output

lastHintExplanation: Node runs the same JavaScript engine as Chrome (V8) but gives it system access (files, network, processes) instead of the DOM. Exit code 0 means success and non-zero means failure; other programs, shell scripts and CI pipelines check it. Writing errors to stderr keeps them separate from normal output that might be piped elsewhere.

title: Files and paths: fs/promises and path
goal: Read and write files safely in Node and build a file-backed notes CLI.

concepts: node:fs/promises: readFile, writeFile, appendFile, mkdir({ recursive }), readdir, stat
node:path: join, resolve, basename, extname, dirname
import.meta.dirname for the current file's folder
Handling ENOENT (file not found) errors
JSON files as a tiny database (and its limits)
Atomic-ish writes: write a temp file, then rename

build.task: In node-playground, build notes.js, a CLI storing notes in data/notes.json: node notes.js add "Buy milk" --tag home; list (optionally --tag home); done <id>; remove <id>; search <text>; stats (total, done, per tag). Create the data folder and file if missing. Handle a corrupted JSON file by backing it up to notes.corrupt-<timestamp>.json and starting fresh. Write the file atomically (temp file + rename). Also write folder-report.js: given a folder path, print the number of files, total size and the 5 biggest files, recursively.
acceptance: All 6 notes commands work, with clear output and usage help
Missing data folder/file is created automatically
Corrupted JSON is backed up and the CLI keeps working
Writes go to a temp file then rename
folder-report.js walks folders recursively and lists the 5 biggest files
Paths built with path.join, not string concatenation

hints: Load: try { return JSON.parse(await readFile(file, 'utf8')); } catch (e) { if (e.code === 'ENOENT') return []; /* else corrupted: back up */ }
Atomic write: await writeFile(file + '.tmp', JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)); await rename(file + '.tmp', file);
Recursive listing: await readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true, recursive: true }), then stat each file for its size.

explainBack.q: Why write to a temp file and rename instead of writing directly?
lookFor: crash mid-write would corrupt the real file
rename is atomic on the same disk
old file stays intact until the new one is complete

explainBack.q: Why use path.join instead of 'data/' + name?
What are the limits of a JSON file as a database?

lastHintExplanation: If the process crashes halfway through writing, the file is left corrupted. Writing to a temp file and then renaming (an atomic operation on the same disk) means the real file is either fully old or fully new. path.join handles OS separators and normalises paths. A JSON file must be rewritten in full on every change and can't handle concurrent writers, which is why we'll use PostgreSQL.

title: Environment variables, npm scripts and TypeScript in Node
goal: Configure Node apps with environment variables and run TypeScript with a fast dev loop.

concepts: Why config lives in environment variables (12-factor app)
.env files with node --env-file=.env (or dotenv); never commit secrets
.env.example to document required variables
Validating config at startup (fail fast with a clear message)
TypeScript in Node: tsx watch for dev, tsc for build
npm scripts: dev, build, start, check

build.task: Create a NEW repo api-starter: a Node + TypeScript project (npm i -D typescript tsx @types/node; strict tsconfig, outDir dist). Write src/config.ts that reads PORT, NODE_ENV, APP_NAME and LOG_LEVEL from process.env, validates them with zod (PORT a number 1–65535, NODE_ENV one of development/test/production) and exits with a readable error listing every problem. Add .env (gitignored) and .env.example. Scripts: dev (tsx watch with --env-file), build (tsc), start (node dist/index.js), check (tsc --noEmit). src/index.ts prints the loaded config, hiding any value whose name contains SECRET or KEY.

starterFiles.name: .env.example
starterFiles.content:
PORT=4000
NODE_ENV=development
APP_NAME=api-starter
LOG_LEVEL=info
# Never commit the real .env file

acceptance: .env is gitignored; .env.example committed
Invalid or missing config prints every problem clearly and exits with code 1
npm run dev reloads on file changes; npm run build and npm start work
Config is typed (z.infer) and imported from one module
Secret-looking values are masked in logs

hints: Dev script: "dev": "tsx watch --env-file=.env src/index.ts". Start: "start": "node --env-file=.env dist/index.js" (or set real environment variables in production).
Env values are always strings. z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535) turns '4000' into 4000.
On failure: const r = schema.safeParse(process.env); if (!r.success) { console.error(r.error.issues.map(i => `${i.path.join('.')}: ${i.message}`).join('\n')); process.exit(1); }

explainBack.q: Why keep config in environment variables instead of in code?
Why validate config at startup instead of when it's first used?
lookFor: fail fast with a clear message

lastHintExplanation: Environment variables let the same code run with different settings in dev, test and production, and keep secrets out of git. Every env value is a string, so validate and coerce it at startup. Failing immediately with a list of what's wrong beats crashing an hour later on the first request that touches a missing setting.

title: HTTP from scratch with node:http
goal: Build a tiny web server without a framework so you understand what Express does for you.

concepts: http.createServer((req, res) => ...) and server.listen(port)
req.method, req.url, req.headers; parsing the URL with new URL()
Writing responses: res.statusCode, res.setHeader, res.end
Reading a request body from a stream (chunks)
Manual routing: if method and path match
Testing with curl, the browser, or a REST client

resources.title: Node.js: Anatomy of an HTTP transaction

build.task: In api-starter, write src/raw-server.ts using only node:http: GET /health → { status: 'ok', uptime }; GET /quotes → list of quotes (in memory), supporting ?author= filter; GET /quotes/:id; POST /quotes with a JSON body (validate text and author, 400 on bad input or invalid JSON); anything else → 404 JSON. Set Content-Type: application/json on every response. Log each request as 'METHOD /path → status (ms)'. Test every route with curl and save the commands and outputs in docs/raw-server.md.
acceptance: All routes work, with correct status codes (200, 201, 400, 404)
?author= filter works (case-insensitive)
Invalid JSON body returns 400, not a crash
Every response is JSON with the right Content-Type
Request log shows method, path, status and duration
docs/raw-server.md has curl commands and real outputs

hints: URL parsing: const url = new URL(req.url ?? '/', `http://${req.headers.host}`); then url.pathname and url.searchParams.get('author').
Body: let raw = ''; for await (const chunk of req) raw += chunk; then try { JSON.parse(raw) } catch { send 400 }.
Timing: const start = performance.now(); res.on('finish', () => console.log(`${req.method} ${url.pathname} → ${res.statusCode} (${Math.round(performance.now() - start)}ms)`));

explainBack.q: Why does reading the request body need a loop or events instead of req.body?
lookFor: body arrives as a stream of chunks

explainBack.q: List three things you had to do by hand that you expect Express to do for you.

lastHintExplanation: HTTP bodies arrive over the network in chunks, so Node exposes the request as a stream; you collect the chunks, then parse them. Writing routing, body parsing, JSON responses and 404 handling yourself shows exactly what Express provides: a router with :params, middleware like express.json(), res.json() and more.

options: The request hangs until it times out
predict.why: The response is never finished, so the client keeps waiting.

title: Express: your first real API server
goal: Rebuild yesterday's server with Express and see how routing, JSON and middleware get simpler.

concepts: express(), app.get/post/put/patch/delete, app.listen
Route params (req.params), query (req.query) and body (req.body)
express.json() middleware to parse JSON bodies
res.json(), res.status(), res.sendStatus()
Middleware: (req, res, next) and order of registration
A 404 handler and an error handler (4 arguments) at the end

build.task: In api-starter (TypeScript), npm i express and npm i -D @types/express. Rebuild the quotes API in src/app.ts with Express: same routes as Day 88, plus PATCH /quotes/:id and DELETE /quotes/:id (204). Write a request-logger middleware, a 404 handler for unknown routes and an error-handling middleware that returns { error } JSON (and hides stack traces in production). Separate app creation (app.ts exports createApp()) from listening (index.ts). Compare line counts with raw-server.ts in docs/express-vs-raw.md.
acceptance: All quote routes work with correct status codes, including 201 for POST and 204 for DELETE
express.json() used; invalid JSON returns a clean 400 from the error handler
Logger, 404 and error middleware registered in the right order
createApp() in app.ts; index.ts only listens
docs/express-vs-raw.md compares the two versions

hints: Order: app.use(logger); app.use(express.json()); routes...; app.use(notFound); app.use(errorHandler). Express checks them top to bottom.
An error handler has 4 parameters: (err, req, res, next) => { ... }. Express only treats it as an error handler if it has all 4.
Invalid JSON: express.json() throws a SyntaxError with status 400. In the error handler, use err.status ?? 500.
proof: Commit with src/app.ts, src/index.ts and docs.

explainBack.q: What is middleware? Explain using your logger.

lookFor: tests can import the app without starting a server

lastHintExplanation: Middleware are functions (req, res, next) that run in the order you register them. Each can read or modify the request, send a response, or call next() to pass control on. The 404 handler goes after all routes, and the 4-argument error handler goes last. Exporting createApp() without listening lets tests use the app directly.

predict.q: app.use(express.json()) is registered AFTER app.post('/quotes', ...). What is req.body in that route?
predict.why: Middleware only runs for routes registered after it.
